option_scores.rationale: Status quo preserves the existing six-week workshop and the invented 12-seat baseline, and it violates no constraint. But it answers nothing about the seat's core question: who wants a group program, how they would find it, and what path converts interest into a purchase. Option A leaves unk-1 (demand for a group program unmeasured) exactly where it is, so the practice pays no cost and also buys no information. Defensible as a holding position, weak as a decision.

A bounded paid pilot is the only listed option that tests the three things this seat exists to test, in the only order that produces usable signal: a defined who, a route by which they hear about it, and an actual transaction that separates real interest from polite interest. The word 'paid' is doing the load-bearing work — free attendance measures willingness to attend, not willingness to buy, and a group program's viability is a purchase question. B is also the only forward option that can satisfy con-1's budget cap and non-displacement requirement, because it is bounded by definition. Scored below 10 because the pilot design is unspecified in the brief and asm-1 (founder-only staffing) is an unverified assumption, so execution risk is real even though the option is correct.

Broad launch commits full delivery, marketing, and support cost against demand that this brief explicitly records as unmeasured (unk-1), while con-1 caps spend to a small invented budget and forbids displacing the existing workshop. C is the option most likely to breach the hard constraint and the least likely to return a clean learning signal, because a broad launch mixes price, audience, and delivery into one number that cannot be attributed. There is no evidence in the manifest supporting launch-scale demand.

framework_applications.application: Build the group program as an offer before building it as a product. Option B should be written down as a single named offer with a specific who, a specific outcome, a price, and a reason to act now — the pilot is the offer's first live test, not a rehearsal for one. If the offer cannot be stated in those terms, the pilot is not ready to run.

The brief asks whether to pilot, but says nothing about how anyone would hear about a group program. A pilot cohort with no defined traffic path to it tests the wrong thing. Before the cohort runs, name one audience already reachable — the invented 12-seat workshop roster is the only audience evidenced in this brief — and one route by which that audience is invited. One audience, one route, then measure.

Price the pilot. A free or heavily discounted cohort returns attendance, which is a weak proxy, and can produce a false positive that then justifies Option C on bad evidence. Set a real price, even a small one, and treat conversion at that price as the pilot's primary result rather than satisfaction scores.

decisive_arguments: Option B is the only option that converts an unmeasured demand question (unk-1) into a measured one, and it does so within the budget cap and non-displacement requirement stated in con-1.
The demand question is a purchase question, not an interest question. Only a paid cohort distinguishes wanting a group program from being willing to buy one.
Option C spends at launch scale against demand this brief records as unmeasured, and is the option most likely to breach the hard constraint in con-1.
Option A is safe but inert: it preserves the 12-seat workshop baseline from fact-1 while leaving the practice with no evidence for or against a group program at any future date.
The pilot is bounded, so its downside is capped by design while its learning value is not.
strongest_objection: The brief never establishes that the existing audience wants a group format at all, and a paid pilot presupposes an audience willing to show up and pay. If the invented workshop graduates want one-to-one attention rather than a group container, the pilot will produce a negative result that is about format preference, not about price or demand — and a practice could wrongly read that negative as proof the group program is unviable rather than as proof the offer was aimed at the wrong who. A stronger sequencing would test format preference cheaply before pricing a cohort, which is a real gap in Option B as currently framed.

conditions.description: The pilot must exist as a single written offer — named who, named outcome, named price, named start date — before any invitation goes out. A cohort assembled without a stated offer cannot be evaluated.
conditions.verification_method: Read the written offer document and confirm all four elements are present and specific; reject any offer with an unnamed audience or an unstated price.
required_evidence: Written pilot offer with audience, outcome, price, and date

conditions.description: One reachable audience and one route of invitation must be named in advance, drawn from people already known to the practice rather than a new cold channel. The invented workshop roster is the only evidenced audience in this brief.
conditions.verification_method: Confirm the audience source and the invite route are documented and that the route does not require spend beyond the con-1 cap.

conditions.description: Pilot spend must be shown to sit inside the small invented budget cap and must be shown not to consume capacity that the existing six-week workshop depends on. This mirrors the hard constraint con-1 and the financial feasibility question raised as an unresolved critical domain.
conditions.verification_method: Compare committed pilot spend against the stated cap and confirm workshop scheduling and staffing remain unchanged for the pilot window.
required_evidence: Workshop schedule for the pilot window

conditions.description: The pilot must carry a real price. A free pilot does not test the purchase question this seat exists to answer, and a positive free-pilot result must not be treated as evidence for Option C.
conditions.verification_method: Confirm the offer states a non-zero price and that results are reported in terms of paid conversions, not attendance.

conditions.description: Option C must not be triggered by pilot completion alone. A stated numeric result at the pilot price, agreed before the cohort starts, is required before any broad launch is considered.
conditions.verification_method: Confirm a pre-agreed numeric threshold exists in writing before the cohort starts and that the launch decision cites that threshold.

conditions.description: Before pricing a full cohort, ask the known audience directly whether they want a group container or continued one-to-one work. This addresses the gap named in the strongest objection and is cheap relative to running the wrong pilot.
conditions.verification_method: Collect and read direct responses from the known audience on format preference before the offer is finalised.
required_evidence: Direct format-preference responses from the known audience

critical_unknowns: FICTIONAL: Whether workshop graduates want a group program at all is unmeasured in this invented case (unk-1).
Whether the fictional pilot is affordable at committed cash levels, raised as an unresolved financial feasibility question tied to con-1.
How any prospective participant would hear about a group program: no traffic source or invitation route is evidenced in this brief.
The price a pilot cohort would bear at all, and therefore whether any conversion figure would be meaningful.
Whether one bounded cohort can be staffed by the founder alone, which is stated only as an assumption (asm-1) and not as evidence.
change_my_mind: I would move off Option B if the format-preference check came back showing the known audience wants one-to-one work rather than a group container — that would mean the pilot tests the wrong thing and the correct move is to re-aim the offer before spending on a cohort. I would move toward Option C if a paid pilot returned conversions at the stated price at or above a threshold agreed in advance, with the workshop schedule and spend cap from con-1 provably intact. I would move toward Option A if the pilot could not clear the con-1 budget cap or could not be run without consuming workshop capacity, since a constraint-breaching pilot is not a cheap test at all.
lenses_used: audience demand and willingness to pay
evidence sufficiency under a single-source manifest
minority_position: If a majority of seats read the demand question as unanswerable from this brief and therefore favour the status quo, the minority position I would hold is that doing nothing is not the neutral choice: Option A is a decision to keep the group program untested indefinitely, and the cost of that decision grows each time the question is deferred. A bounded, priced pilot with a pre-agreed numeric stop rule carries capped downside and is cheaper than another cycle of not knowing.
